key_terms.meaning: A context-free grammar with a semantic rule attached to each production; the rules say how each attribute of each grammar symbol is computed.
The expression attached to a production that computes an attribute value, e.g. E.val = E₁.val + T.val.
An attribute whose value at a node is computed from the attribute values of that node's children; information flows upward.
An attribute whose value at a node is computed from the parent's or siblings' attribute values; information flows downward or sideways.
A parse tree in which every node shows the values of its attributes.
A graph whose nodes are attributes and whose edges say 'this attribute needs that one'; a topological order of it gives a safe evaluation order.
A parse tree with keywords, semicolons, parentheses and single-child chains removed; each interior node is an operator, each leaf is an operand.
A syntax tree in which two nodes with the same operator and the same children point to one shared node, so each distinct subexpression appears once.
A term naming a type, built from basic type names, type variables and type constructors such as array, ↑ (pointer) and → (function).
The collection of rules that assign a type expression to every part of a program and decide whether each construct is well typed.
Verifying that every operator, assignment and call receives operands whose type expressions are allowed by the language rules.
A machine-independent form of the program produced by the front end and consumed by the back end.
A linear form in which each operator follows its operands, e.g. ab+; no parentheses and no precedence rules are needed.
A sequence of instructions of the form x = y op z, where each instruction has at most one operator and at most three names.
A four-field row (op, arg1, arg2, result) that stores one three-address instruction in a table.
A three-field row (op, arg1, arg2) where a result is referred to by its row number instead of a name.
An array of triples plus a separate list of pointers to them, so the triples can be reordered without rewriting their references.
A table mapping each declared name to its type expression, width in bytes and relative address.
Leaving a jump target blank, keeping that instruction on a list, and filling in the real label number later when it is known.
Evaluating a && b or a || b from left to right and stopping as soon as the result is fixed.

takeaways: An SDD is a grammar plus semantic rules; synthesized attributes move information up the tree, inherited attributes move it down or across.
Attribute evaluation must follow the dependency graph, and a topological order of that graph always gives a legal order.
Dropping punctuation from a parse tree gives a syntax tree; additionally sharing identical subexpressions gives a DAG.
A DAG is worth building because every shared node is a common subexpression that the later code need not recompute.
Type expressions let the compiler store types as small trees and check each use by structural comparison.
Postfix is the simplest linear intermediate form: it is evaluated with one stack and needs no parentheses.
Three-address code is the usual middle form because it is linear like machine code but free of machine details.
Quadruples name their results, triples do not, and indirect triples add a pointer array so that instructions can be moved.
Declarations only build the symbol table; assignment statements are the first place real code is emitted, and array elements need an address formula.
Boolean expressions are translated as jumps, and backpatching fills in jump targets in one forward pass without going back.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask you to take a given grammar or code fragment, write the semantic rules or the three-address code, and show the intermediate table or the patched jumps — so practise full worked traces, not just definitions.

bank.q: Define synthesized and inherited attributes. Explain, with a small grammar, how each is computed and in what order attributes can be evaluated.
outline: Definition of an attribute as a property of a grammar symbol
Synthesized: value from children only; bottom-up evaluation
Inherited: value from parent or siblings; needs top-down or left-to-right order
Worked SDD for E → E + T with a val attribute
Dependency graph and topological order as the general evaluation rule

bank.q: Explain how a syntax tree is obtained from a parse tree and how a DAG is obtained from a syntax tree. Illustrate with the expression (a + b) * (a + b) * c.
outline: Parse tree contains nonterminals, keywords and punctuation
Remove single-child chains and punctuation; operators become interior nodes
DAG: merge nodes with identical operator and identical children
Worked drawing showing the shared (a + b) node
Why sharing saves work later (common subexpression elimination)

bank.q: What is a type expression? Give the type expressions for a two-dimensional integer array, a pointer to a real, and a function from integer to integer. Explain how type checking uses them.
outline: Type expression built from basic types, type variables and constructors
array(2, array(3, integer)) for a 2×3 integer array
pointer(real) and integer → integer
Structural equality of type expressions
Rules for expressions, assignment compatibility and error reporting

bank.q: Compare quadruples, triples and indirect triples with the same set of three-address instructions.
outline: Quadruple: op, arg1, arg2, result; results are named temporaries
Triple: op, arg1, arg2 with result referred to by row position
Indirect triple: array of pointers into the triple table
Effect of inserting or reordering an instruction in each scheme
Space and ease-of-optimisation trade-off

bank.q: Write postfix equivalents for a + b * c, (a + b) * (c − d) and −a + b. State two advantages of postfix as an intermediate form.
outline: abc*+
ab+cd−*
a−b+ (unary minus first)
No parentheses and no precedence needed
Direct evaluation with a stack; easy to generate from a bottom-up parse

bank.q: For the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | id, write an SDD and show the annotated parse tree for id + id * id.
outline: Semantic rule for each production, with val and lexval
Nodes annotated with values or with pointers to symbol-table entries
Correct left-to-right order of evaluation
Final tree with the root attribute value

bank.q: Generate three-address code for the statement a[i][j] = b + c, assuming row-major layout, 4 bytes per element, and i, j starting at 1. Show every temporary.
outline: Formula base + ((i − low₁) × n₂ + (j − low₂)) × w
Compute t1 = i − 1, t2 = j − 1, t3 = t1 × n₂, t4 = t3 + t2, t5 = t4 × 4
Address t6 = base_a + t5, then a[t6] = t7
Fetch b and c, add into a temporary
Correct use of widths and of the lower bounds

bank.q: Translate if x < y then s1 else s2 and while x < y do s into three-address code using backpatching. Show the lists truelist, falselist and nextlist at each step.
outline: Boolean test compiled as conditional and unconditional jumps
if: test, jump-if-false to the else part, then part, jump to end
while: label at the test, body, jump back to the test
makelist, merge and backpatch operations on the lists
Final code with every label filled in

bank.q: Show the quadruple table for the code d = (a + b) * (a + b) − c. How would the same code look as triples and as indirect triples?
outline: Three temporaries named with the arithmetic
Quadruples with op, arg1, arg2, result
Triples referencing (1) or (2) in the argument fields
Indirect triples with row 35 pointing to triple 1 and so on
Note that the repeated (a + b) is computed once

bank.q: Write the semantic actions that enter a declaration such as int a[10][20]; into the symbol table, and state what is stored for the name a.
outline: Actions after the type and after each declarator
Type expression array(10, array(20, integer))
Width = 10 × 20 × 4 = 800 bytes
Relative address from the current offset, offset then increased
Storage class, base, and low/high bounds kept in the entry

bank.q: Why is backpatching preferred over a two-pass generation of jump targets? Explain the list operations makelist, merge and backpatch with an example.
outline: One forward pass over the syntax tree
Targets unknown when the jump is emitted
Each instruction carries a list of incomplete jumps
makelist creates a one-element list, merge concatenates, backpatch fills label numbers
Example with while and short-circuit and/or showing saved lists

bank.q: Discuss the properties a good intermediate representation should have. Compare postfix, syntax trees and three-address code against those properties.
outline: Machine independence, ease of generation, ease of optimisation, compactness
Postfix: linear, stack-friendly, weak for reordering
Tree/DAG: exposes structure and sharing, not linear
Three-address code: linear like machine code, exposes temporaries and control flow
Choice depends on the optimiser and the target

bank.q: Take the grammar of a small language with declarations, assignment, an if-else and a while. Write syntax-directed rules and produce the complete three-address code for one sample program that uses all four constructs.
outline: Declaration rules update the symbol table and offset
Assignment rules emit address and value code
Conditional rules build truelist and falselist
Loop rules emit a label at the test and a backward jump
A clean final listing with labels L1, L2 and temporaries t1, t2

bank.q: Explain the rules for type checking expressions and statements in a language with integer, real, array and pointer types. Discuss one case where the checker must insert a conversion and one where it must report an error.
outline: Type expressions and structural equality
Rules for arithmetic with widening from integer to real
Assignment compatibility and the narrowing question
Array index must be an integer, pointer dereference must be a pointer
Error example a[i] where a is integer; conversion example x = y + 1 with x real

glossary.meaning: A property of a grammar symbol at one node of a parse tree, such as its value, type or place.
A grammar whose productions each carry semantic rules for computing attributes.
A grammar with program fragments placed inside the right side of productions, run in the order the symbols are matched.
An SDD that uses only synthesized attributes, so it can be evaluated in one bottom-up pass.
An SDD whose inherited attributes depend only on the parent and on siblings to the left, so it can be evaluated in one left-to-right pass.
A parse tree with attribute values written beside each node.
A directed graph linking each attribute to the attributes its value depends on.
Two occurrences of the same operator applied to the same operands, computed once and shared.
A node of a syntax tree that stands for an operator and has children for its operands.
A type-building operator such as array, pointer or function arrow.
Deciding types at compile time, before the program runs.
Working out an expression's type from the types of its parts using the language's rules.
Any machine-independent notation, such as postfix or three-address code, used between the front end and the back end.
An abstract machine whose instructions push and pop operands on a single stack; the natural executor of postfix code.
A compiler-generated name, usually t1, t2, …, that holds one intermediate result.
An array of rows, each holding one three-address instruction, indexed by row number.
One row of the symbol table holding a name, its type expression, its width and its offset.
The number of bytes a variable of a given type occupies in memory.
The byte distance of a variable from the base of its storage area.
A name attached to an instruction so that jumps can refer to it.
The label or address a conditional or unconditional jump transfers control to.
A list of positions of instructions whose jump target is still unknown.
Reaching the next instruction in sequence without a jump.
The order in which statements execute, decided by tests, loops and calls.
